jermak-beginnt-die-eroberung-sibiriens#t: The Stroganov merchant family recruited Cossacks under their leader Yermak to protect their estates in the Urals. In 1582 Yermak crossed the mountains with a few hundred men and captured Qashliq, the capital of Khan Kuchum. Yermak was killed in 1585, but the tsar sent more troops and had fortresses such as Tobolsk built. Lured by the valuable fur of the sable, Cossacks and traders moved east along the rivers and reached the Pacific in 1639. The indigenous peoples had to pay tribute in furs.
spanische-armada#title: The defeat of the Spanish Armada
spanische-armada#summary: Philip II's invasion fleet fails in the English Channel against the English fleet and against storms; England holds its own as a Protestant sea power.
spanische-armada#text: With around 130 ships Philip II intended to ferry an army from the Netherlands to England in order to overthrow Elizabeth I and restore Catholicism. The more maneuverable English ships under Howard and Drake fired on the Armada from a distance, fireships broke up its formation off Calais, and at Gravelines it suffered heavy losses. On the way home around Scotland and Ireland, storms destroyed a large part of the fleet; only about two thirds of the ships returned. The victory consolidated Elizabeth's rule, strengthened English self-confidence, and set in motion England's rise as a sea power.
schlacht-von-tondibi#title: Battle of Tondibi and the end of the Songhai Empire
schlacht-von-tondibi#summary: A Moroccan army with firearms crosses the Sahara and defeats the army of Songhai.
schlacht-von-tondibi#text: The Moroccan sultan Ahmad al-Mansur wanted to bring the gold sources of West Africa under his control. He sent an army of a few thousand men under the Spanish-born commander Judar Pasha across the Sahara. At Tondibi near Gao, in March 1591, the troops, armed with muskets and cannon, met the far larger army of Askia Ishaq II and defeated it. Songhai fell apart, Timbuktu and Gao came under Moroccan rule, and leading scholars were deported to Marrakesh. The hoped-for quantities of gold never reached Morocco, however, and the region broke up into smaller lordships.
imjin-krieg#title: The Imjin War: Japan's invasion of Korea
imjin-krieg#summary: Toyotomi Hideyoshi has Korea attacked in order to conquer China but fails against Korean resistance, Yi Sun-sin's fleet and Ming troops.
imjin-krieg#text: After unifying Japan, Hideyoshi planned the conquest of China and demanded free passage from Korea. In 1592 more than 150,000 men landed at Busan and within a few weeks took Seoul and Pyongyang. Admiral Yi Sun-sin, however, cut the invaders' supply lines with his ships, including armoured turtle ships, and a Ming army came to Korea's aid. A second attack in 1597 also stalled. After Hideyoshi's death in 1598 the Japanese withdrew; Korea was badly devastated.
isfahan-wird-hauptstadt#title: Abbas I makes Isfahan his capital
isfahan-wird-hauptstadt#summary: Shah Abbas I moves the Safavid capital to Isfahan and has it developed into one of the most splendid cities in the world.
isfahan-wird-hauptstadt#text: Abbas I had strengthened an empire hard pressed by the Ottomans and Uzbeks through reforms, and in 1598 he made Isfahan the seat of government. Around the vast Naqsh-e Jahan square rose the Ali Qapu palace, the Shah Mosque and the Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque with their domes of blue tiles. Gardens, bridges and a covered bazaar made the city famous; a Persian saying called Isfahan half the world. Armenian merchants, whom Abbas settled in the suburb of New Julfa, managed the lucrative silk trade.
schlacht-von-sekigahara#summary: Tokugawa Ieyasu defeats the coalition of his rivals and lays the foundation for the Tokugawa shogunate, which rules Japan until 1868.
schlacht-von-sekigahara#text: After the death of Toyotomi Hideyoshi in 1598 the most powerful lords of Japan fought for supremacy. In October 1600 the Eastern Army under Tokugawa Ieyasu and the Western Army under Ishida Mitsunari clashed at Sekigahara. When several lords changed sides during the battle, Ieyasu won. In 1603 the emperor appointed him shogun, and Edo became the centre of power. With the capture of Osaka Castle in 1615 Ieyasu eliminated the last supporters of the Toyotomi.
quilombo-dos-palmares#summary: In north-eastern Brazil the largest community of escaped enslaved people holds out for almost a century.
quilombo-dos-palmares#text: From the beginning of the 17th century enslaved people fled from the sugar plantations of Pernambuco into the forested hills of the Serra da Barriga. There Palmares arose, a federation of villages in which, according to estimates, several thousand people lived from farming, hunting and trade. The inhabitants repelled numerous attacks by Dutch and Portuguese troops. The leader Zumbi rejected a peace offer of 1678 because it left slavery outside Palmares untouched. In 1694 an army under Domingos Jorge Velho captured the main settlement, and Zumbi was killed the following year.
jesuitenreduktionen-in-paraguay#title: Beginning of the Jesuit reductions in Paraguay
jesuitenreduktionen-in-paraguay#summary: Jesuits found the first mission villages for the Guaraní on the Paraná, which soon form a large network.
jesuitenreduktionen-in-paraguay#text: In the reductions the Guaraní lived in planned villages with a church, workshops and jointly farmed fields under the direction of a few Jesuit fathers. The inhabitants were protected from the encomienda but had to follow Christian rules of life. Against slave raiders from São Paulo, the bandeirantes, the villages were allowed to defend themselves with militias of their own. At their peak in the 18th century well over a hundred thousand people lived in some thirty reductions. Music, wood carving and a written form of Guaraní flourished there.
dreissigjaehriger-krieg#summary: A war of religion and power devastates the Holy Roman Empire and draws in almost all the European powers.
dreissigjaehriger-krieg#text: The war began with the Defenestration of Prague, when Protestant Bohemian nobles threw imperial governors out of a window. After victories by the emperor, Denmark, Sweden under Gustavus Adolphus, and finally Catholic France intervened on the Protestant side. Mercenary armies, hunger, and epidemics killed more than a third of the population in some regions of Germany.
njinga-verhandelt-in-luanda#title: Njinga negotiates with the Portuguese in Luanda
njinga-verhandelt-in-luanda#summary: As her brother's envoy, Njinga negotiates with the Portuguese governor of Angola for peace for the kingdom of Ndongo.
njinga-verhandelt-in-luanda#text: The kingdom of Ndongo in what is now Angola suffered from the campaigns of the Portuguese, who hunted captives for the slave trade from Luanda. In 1622 Njinga, the king's sister, travelled to Luanda and negotiated a peace treaty. According to a well-known tradition, when she was offered no chair she sat on the back of a servant so as to meet the governor as an equal. She was baptized, but the Portuguese did not keep the treaty. From 1624 Njinga ruled herself and for decades waged war and diplomacy against the colonial power.
koesem-sultan-regentschaft#summary: When her son Murad IV becomes sultan as a child, the sultan's mother Kösem effectively governs the empire.
koesem-sultan-regentschaft#text: In September 1623 the eleven-year-old Murad IV was placed on the throne, and his mother Kösem conducted the business of government as valide sultan. She negotiated with viziers and Janissaries and secured the throne in a time of revolts and war with Persia. Only around 1632 did Murad take power himself. After his death in 1640 Kösem governed again for her son Ibrahim and from 1648 for her grandson Mehmed IV. Historians call this period of great influence of the palace women the "Sultanate of Women".
hoehepunkt-der-hexenverfolgung#title: The height of the witch hunts
hoehepunkt-der-hexenverfolgung#summary: In the years around 1630 the witch trials in central Europe reach their peak, with thousands of executions.
hoehepunkt-der-hexenverfolgung#text: Between about 1560 and 1630, tens of thousands of people in Europe were accused as witches, forced under torture to confess, and burned; most of the victims were women, and many trials took place in the prince-bishoprics of Würzburg, Bamberg, and Cologne. The hardship of war, crop failures, and the expectation that the devil worked harm with the help of witches fueled the persecution. In 1631 the Jesuit Friedrich Spee criticized torture in the Cautio Criminalis as a source of false confessions. The trials ended only in the 18th century; the last execution in Europe took place in Switzerland in 1782.
bau-des-taj-mahal#summary: The Great Mughal Shah Jahan has a tomb of white marble built in Agra for his late wife Mumtaz Mahal.
bau-des-taj-mahal#text: Mumtaz Mahal, Shah Jahan's favourite wife, died in 1631 giving birth to her fourteenth child. The following year work began on the banks of the Yamuna in Agra on a mausoleum built by thousands of craftsmen from India, Persia and Central Asia. The white marble was inlaid with semi-precious stones and decorated with Quranic verses in calligraphy. The gardens, mosque and guest house were completed around 1653. The Taj Mahal is regarded as the high point of Mughal architecture and is now a World Heritage Site.
galileis-prozess#summary: The Roman Inquisition condemns Galileo for his defense of the heliocentric model and forces him to recant.
galileis-prozess#text: In his Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems of 1632, Galileo had presented the teaching of Copernicus so convincingly that the church saw in it a violation of the prohibition of 1616. On 22 June 1633, almost seventy years old, he had to abjure on his knees in Rome and was sentenced to lifelong house arrest. In his villa near Florence he nevertheless wrote the Discorsi on mechanics and the laws of falling bodies, which appeared in the Netherlands in 1638. The trial became a symbol of the conflict between science and the authority of faith; the church rehabilitated Galileo only in 1992.
abschliessung-japans#title: The closing of Japan under the Tokugawa
abschliessung-japans#summary: The Tokugawa shogunate bars the Portuguese from entering, forbids Japanese to leave the country, and allows only the Dutch and the Chinese limited trade, which is soon confined entirely to Nagasaki.
abschliessung-japans#text: Tokugawa Ieyasu had founded the shogunate in 1603 and pacified Japan after a century of civil war. His successors feared that Christian missionaries and European traders might undermine the established order, especially since a revolt of Christian peasants at Shimabara had to be bloodily put down in 1637. Through a series of decrees between 1633 and 1639, Christianity was banned, the building of ocean-going ships was forbidden, and the Portuguese were expelled; in 1641 the Dutch were moved to the artificial island of Dejima off Nagasaki. This policy, known as sakoku, lasted until 1854 and gave Japan more than two centuries of peace and a culture of its own.
evliya-celebis-reisen#summary: Evliya Çelebi of Istanbul travels through the Ottoman Empire and its neighbours for four decades and describes them in ten volumes.
evliya-celebis-reisen#text: In 1640 Evliya Çelebi began by describing Istanbul and then Bursa, and afterwards set out on journeys that until 1682 took him from Bosnia to the Caucasus, to Vienna, Mecca, Cairo and the Sudan. He often accompanied embassies and governors and wrote about cities, buildings, languages, foods, customs and crafts. His "Book of Travels" (Seyahatname) mixes precise observation with anecdotes and exaggerations. It is one of the most important sources for everyday life in the 17th century.
englischer-buergerkrieg#title: The English Civil War and the execution of Charles I
englischer-buergerkrieg#summary: In the struggle between king and parliament the parliamentary army wins; in 1649 Charles I becomes the first European monarch to be executed in public.
englischer-buergerkrieg#text: Charles I had ruled for eleven years without parliament and had tried to force an episcopal church on Scotland, until lack of money compelled him to summon parliament in 1640. The dispute over taxes, religion, and command of the army escalated into civil war in 1642 between royalists and parliamentary troops, in which Oliver Cromwell's New Model Army forced the decision at Naseby in 1645. A parliament purged by the army condemned the king for high treason, and on 30 January 1649 he was beheaded in front of his palace in London. England became a republic, and from 1653 a protectorate under Cromwell; in 1660 the monarchy returned under Charles II.
mandschu-erobern-peking#title: The Manchus take Beijing: the beginning of the Qing dynasty
mandschu-erobern-peking#summary: After rebels overthrow the Ming, the Manchus enter Beijing and found the Qing dynasty, the last imperial dynasty of China.
mandschu-erobern-peking#text: Famines, empty treasuries and peasant uprisings had weakened the Ming. In April 1644 the rebel leader Li Zicheng took Beijing, and the last Ming emperor hanged himself. The Ming general Wu Sangui then opened the Shanhaiguan pass to the Manchus, who drove out Li Zicheng and took the throne themselves. The Manchus forced Chinese men to adopt their hairstyle with a shaved forehead and a queue. Resistance in the south lasted for decades until Taiwan was conquered in 1683.
westfaelischer-frieden#summary: In Münster and Osnabrück the first great European peace congress brings the Thirty Years' War to an end.
westfaelischer-frieden#text: After five years of negotiations, Catholics, Lutherans, and Calvinists in the empire received equal rights, and the territorial rulers gained far-reaching sovereignty. France and Sweden received territories, and the independence of the Netherlands and of Switzerland was recognized. The peace is regarded as the birth of the modern system of states, in which sovereign states regulate their relations by treaty.
herrschaft-aurangzebs#title: Aurangzeb's rule over the Mughal Empire
herrschaft-aurangzebs#summary: Aurangzeb brings the Mughal Empire to its greatest extent, but endless wars and religious tensions pave the way for its collapse.
herrschaft-aurangzebs#text: In 1658 Aurangzeb prevailed in the struggle against his brothers and had his father Shah Jahan confined in Agra Fort until his death. As a devout Sunni he reintroduced the special tax on non-Muslims in 1679 and sponsored a compilation of Islamic law. He conquered the sultanates of Bijapur and Golconda in the Deccan, so that the empire covered almost the entire subcontinent. Against the Marathas under Shivaji and his successors, however, he waged war for decades. After his death in 1707 the empire disintegrated rapidly.
gruendung-der-royal-society#summary: In London, scholars found a society for the advancement of scientific knowledge through experiment and exchange.
gruendung-der-royal-society#text: After a lecture by the architect Christopher Wren, twelve men, among them Robert Boyle, resolved on 28 November 1660 to form a society for the advancement of knowledge about nature; in 1662 it received a royal charter. Its motto Nullius in verba, on no one's word, expressed the principle that only experiment and observation should count as proof. From 1665 the Philosophical Transactions appeared, the oldest scientific journal still in existence, and Robert Hooke as curator demonstrated experiments every week. Newton headed the society from 1703 until his death; academies in Paris, Berlin, and St Petersburg were founded on its model.
schlacht-von-mbwila#summary: Portuguese troops from Angola defeat the army of the kingdom of Kongo and kill King António I.
schlacht-von-mbwila#text: In the 17th century relations between Kongo and the Portuguese colony of Angola deteriorated because of border disputes and the struggle over mineral resources. In October 1665 a battle took place at Mbwila, in which a Portuguese army with many African auxiliaries defeated the forces of Kongo. King António I was killed, and his head was taken to Luanda. In the following decades Kongo disintegrated in civil wars between rival noble families, in which many captives were drawn into the slave trade. Only at the beginning of the 18th century was the kingdom reunited, though with greatly diminished power.
hof-nach-versailles#title: Louis XIV moves the court to Versailles
hof-nach-versailles#summary: The Sun King makes the magnificent palace of Versailles the permanent seat of government and court.
hof-nach-versailles#text: Out of a hunting lodge belonging to his father, Louis XIV had an enormous complex built over decades, with the Hall of Mirrors and its gardens. The nobility was tied to the court, where it competed for the king's favor in a strictly regulated ceremonial and was thereby deprived of political power. Versailles became the model for palaces throughout Europe and a symbol of absolutism.
belagerung-wiens-1683#title: The second siege of Vienna by the Ottomans
belagerung-wiens-1683#summary: A relief army under the Polish king John III Sobieski defeats the Ottoman army before Vienna and begins the Ottoman withdrawal from central Europe.
belagerung-wiens-1683#text: In July 1683 the grand vizier Kara Mustafa encircled Vienna with around 150,000 men, and the garrison and citizens held the city for two months while Emperor Leopold I had fled. On 12 September an army of imperial, Polish, Bavarian, and Saxon troops attacked down from the Kahlenberg; the charge of the Polish cavalry decided the battle. In the Great Turkish War that followed, the Habsburgs conquered Hungary and Transylvania, which the Treaty of Karlowitz confirmed in 1699. Austria thus became a great power in southeastern Europe, and Ottoman expansion in Europe was at an end.
edikt-von-fontainebleau#title: Edict of Fontainebleau: the expulsion of the Huguenots
edikt-von-fontainebleau#summary: Louis XIV revokes the Edict of Nantes and forbids Protestant worship in France; hundreds of thousands of Huguenots flee.
edikt-von-fontainebleau#text: For the Sun King, the unity of the state included the unity of faith, and even before 1685 billeted dragoons had forced Protestant families to convert. The edict of October 1685 had the churches of the Huguenots torn down, banished their pastors, and at the same time forbade the faithful to emigrate. Nevertheless some 200,000 people fled, many of them craftsmen, merchants, and officers, to the Netherlands, England, Switzerland, and Brandenburg, which invited them with the Edict of Potsdam. France lost valuable skilled workers, and the thinkers of the Enlightenment saw in the edict an example of the consequences of religious intolerance.
newtons-principia#summary: With the laws of motion and the law of gravitation, Isaac Newton founds classical physics.
newtons-principia#text: In the Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, Newton showed that the same force makes an apple fall to the ground and holds the moon in its orbit. The movements of the planets, the tides, and the trajectory of projectiles could now be calculated with a few mathematical laws. The work became the model for a science that understands nature as governed by law and open to calculation.
genroku-kultur-in-japan#title: The flowering of Genroku culture in Japan
genroku-kultur-in-japan#summary: In the cities of the Edo period a lively urban culture emerges with kabuki, puppet theatre, haiku, novels and woodblock prints.
genroku-kultur-in-japan#text: The long peace under the Tokugawa allowed cities such as Edo, Osaka and Kyoto to grow, and wealthy merchants there developed a lifestyle of their own. In the Genroku period Ihara Saikaku wrote novels about love and money, and Chikamatsu Monzaemon wrote plays for puppet theatre and kabuki. Matsuo Bashō made the short haiku poem a recognized art and in 1689 walked to the north of Japan. Artists began to print pictures of the floating world of the pleasure quarters as woodblock prints. This art form influenced European painters in the 19th century.
glorious-revolution#summary: The English parliament drives out the Catholic king James II and establishes the supremacy of parliament.
glorious-revolution#text: Parliament called the Protestant William of Orange and his wife Mary into the country, whereupon James II fled to France almost without a fight. In 1689 the new rulers had to accept the Bill of Rights, which secured for parliament the right to grant taxes, free elections, and freedom of speech. England thus became a constitutional monarchy and a counter-model to absolutism.
lockes-two-treatises#title: Locke publishes the Two Treatises of Government
lockes-two-treatises#summary: John Locke bases rule on the consent of the governed and on the protection of life, liberty, and property.
lockes-two-treatises#text: Shortly after the Glorious Revolution, Locke's Two Treatises of Government appeared anonymously, in which he refuted the doctrine of the divine right of kings. Human beings, he argued, are by nature free and equal and join together in a state only in order to secure their natural rights; a government that violates these rights may be removed. In the same year his Letter Concerning Toleration appeared, and his Essay Concerning Human Understanding, which traced all knowledge back to experience. Locke's ideas shaped the American Declaration of Independence and liberal political theory to this day.
vertrag-von-nertschinsk#summary: After border fighting on the Amur, Russia and Qing China fix their border by treaty for the first time.
vertrag-von-nertschinsk#text: Russian Cossacks had built forts such as Albazin on the Amur, which were besieged by troops of the Kangxi emperor. In 1689 envoys of both empires negotiated at Nerchinsk east of Lake Baikal; Jesuits served as interpreters, and the binding text was drawn up in Latin. Russia gave up the Amur region and in return received the right to trade with China. The treaty was the first that China concluded with a European state on an equal footing. The border held until the middle of the 19th century.
sor-juana-antwort-an-sor-filotea#summary: The Mexican nun and poet Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz defends the right of women to knowledge and study.
sor-juana-antwort-an-sor-filotea#text: In 1690 the Bishop of Puebla had published a theological text by Sor Juana and, under the pseudonym Sor Filotea, at the same time admonished her to devote herself to pious rather than worldly studies. In her reply of 1691 Sor Juana described her lifelong thirst for knowledge and invoked learned women of the Bible and of antiquity. She argued that education did not lead women away from faith but deepened it. The text is regarded as one of the earliest writings in the Americas to justify the right of women to education. A few years later Sor Juana gave up her library.
goldrausch-in-minas-gerais#summary: Gold finds in the interior of Brazil set off a wave of migration and shift the colony's centre of gravity to the south.
goldrausch-in-minas-gerais#text: In the 1690s bandeirantes from São Paulo found rich gold deposits in the mountains of what later became Minas Gerais. Tens of thousands of Portuguese and Brazilians moved to the new mining towns such as Vila Rica, today's Ouro Preto, and large numbers of enslaved Africans were brought with them into the mines. In the 18th century diamond finds followed. Much of the gold flowed via Portugal to England. In 1763 the capital was moved from Salvador to Rio de Janeiro, the port of the gold region.
frieden-von-karlowitz#summary: After the Great Turkish War the Ottoman Empire cedes Hungary and Transylvania to the Habsburgs – the beginning of the retreat from central Europe.
frieden-von-karlowitz#text: After the failed siege of Vienna in 1683, the Habsburgs, Poland, Venice and Russia had fought the Ottomans in the Holy League; Prince Eugene won at Zenta in 1697. On 26 January 1699 peace was concluded at Karlowitz in Syrmia. The Habsburgs received almost all of Hungary and Transylvania, Venice the Peloponnese and Poland Podolia. For the first time the Ottomans accepted the mediation of foreign envoys and fixed borders. The treaty marks the end of Ottoman expansion in Europe.
osei-tutu-gruendet-asante#title: Osei Tutu founds the Asante Empire
osei-tutu-gruendet-asante#summary: With the victory over Denkyira at Feyiase and the symbol of the Golden Stool, Osei Tutu unites the Akan states into the Asante Empire.
osei-tutu-gruendet-asante#text: In the late 17th century several Akan states in the forest zone of present-day Ghana joined together under Osei Tutu, the ruler of Kumasi. According to tradition, the priest Okomfo Anokye caused a golden stool to descend from the sky, which from then on embodied the soul and unity of the people. Around 1701 the Asante defeated the kingdom of Denkyira, to which they had until then paid tribute, at Feyiase. Osei Tutu became the first asantehene, and Kumasi developed into the capital of an empire that traded in gold, kola nuts and captives. Asante remained one of the strongest powers in West Africa until the late 19th century.
gruendung-st-petersburgs#title: Peter the Great founds St Petersburg
gruendung-st-petersburgs#summary: In the marshland on the Neva, the tsar has a new capital built as a window on Europe.
gruendung-st-petersburgs#text: During the Great Northern War against Sweden, Peter I laid out the Peter and Paul Fortress on conquered land by the Baltic, and from it the city grew. Tens of thousands of forced laborers died during the building work on the marshy ground. In 1712 St Petersburg became the capital of Russia and remained so until 1918; the city symbolized the opening of the empire to the west.
tulpenzeit#summary: Under Ahmed III and his grand vizier Damad İbrahim Pasha, Istanbul experiences a time of peace full of festivities, gardens and curiosity about Europe.
tulpenzeit#text: After the Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718 the grand vizier Nevşehirli Damad İbrahim Pasha relied on diplomacy and splendour. Palaces and gardens such as Sadabad arose on the Golden Horn, tulip bulbs became coveted luxury goods, and the court celebrated festivals of lights. An envoy reported from Paris on Versailles in 1720/21, and in 1727 the first press for Turkish books was set up. The extravagance and new taxes aroused discontent: in 1730 the revolt of Patrona Halil toppled the grand vizier and Sultan Ahmed III. The name "Tulip Period" was only coined by writers of the 20th century.
dahomey-erobert-ouidah#title: Dahomey conquers the slave port of Ouidah
dahomey-erobert-ouidah#summary: King Agaja of Dahomey conquers the coastal town of Ouidah and secures direct trade with the Europeans for his kingdom.
dahomey-erobert-ouidah#text: Dahomey, with its capital Abomey, lay in the hinterland of the so-called Slave Coast in present-day Benin. King Agaja conquered the kingdom of Allada in 1724 and in 1727 the port of Ouidah, one of the most important hubs of the Atlantic slave trade. Dahomey sold prisoners of war to European traders and received firearms, cloth and cowrie shells in return. The state was tightly organized, and a corps of female warriors, called Amazons by Europeans, formed part of its army. Until the 19th century hundreds of thousands of people were carried off from Ouidah to the Americas.
erste-osmanische-druckerei#title: Müteferrika founds the first Turkish printing press
erste-osmanische-druckerei#summary: İbrahim Müteferrika receives the sultan's permission to print books in Ottoman Turkish with Arabic type.
erste-osmanische-druckerei#text: Jewish printers had been working in the empire since the late 15th century, Armenian and Greek printers since the 16th and 17th centuries, but books in Arabic script continued to be copied by hand. In 1727 İbrahim Müteferrika and Said Efendi received a decree from the sultan and an approving opinion from the şeyhülislam; religious texts remained excluded. In 1729 the first book appeared, an Arabic-Turkish dictionary. By 1742 Müteferrika had printed 17 works, among them histories, maps and a treatise on military reform. A broad book market only emerged in the 19th century.
oyo-macht-dahomey-tributpflichtig#title: Oyo forces Dahomey to pay tribute
oyo-macht-dahomey-tributpflichtig#summar: After several campaigns by its cavalry, the Yoruba empire of Oyo makes the kingdom of Dahomey its tributary.
oyo-macht-dahomey-tributpflichtig#text: Oyo, in the savanna north of the rainforest, was the most powerful Yoruba state in the 17th and 18th centuries. Its strength rested on a large cavalry whose horses were imported from the north. After repeated invasions of Dahomey, King Agaja had to recognize Oyo's overlordship around 1730 and pay annual tribute. The alaafin, the king of Oyo, ruled together with a council of nobles, the Oyo Mesi, which could even force him to commit suicide. In the early 19th century Oyo broke apart through internal power struggles and attacks from the north.
qianlong-bluete-der-qing#title: The Qianlong Emperor and the height of the Qing dynasty
qianlong-bluete-der-qing#summary: Under the Qianlong Emperor, China reaches its greatest extent and a golden age of culture.
